title: Half-Truths Break Similarity-Based Retrieval
claim: Adding one plausible but incorrect detail to a correct description raises similarity in standard models, while ours correctly penalizes it.
layout: Top: image plus anchor→two foils flow; bottom: three bar-chart panels, cut off
description: The top row shows a photo of two elephants beside a wooden log, labeled "Image". To its right, a green rounded box labeled "Anchor" contains the word "log". Two arrows lead from it to an orange box (HT1: "log and zebras") and a purple box (HT2: "elephants are away from log"). Below are three side-by-side bar-chart panels titled "CLIP ✗", "NegCLIP ✗" and "CS-CLIP ✓". Each panel has green, orange and purple bars for anchor, HT1 and HT2 similarity, with values written above the bars. A dashed green line marks the anchor level. In CLIP and NegCLIP the purple half-truth bar is tallest (0.29). In CS-CLIP the green anchor bar is tallest (0.30) and the half-truths score lower. Color coding ties the text boxes to the bars. The image is cut off at the bottom: the bars' lower portions and the x-axis are missing.
caption: The half-truth vulnerability. Starting from a short, caption-supported description (the anchor), we form a half-truth by adding one realistic but incorrect detail. CLIP and NegCLIP assign higher similarity to the half-truth, while CS-CLIP (ours) correctly penalizes the incorrect addition.
abstract: When a text description is extended with an additional detail, image-text similarity should drop if that detail is wrong. We show that CLIP-style dual encoders often violate this intuition: appending a plausible but incorrect object or relation to an otherwise correct description can increase the similarity score. We call such cases half-truths. On COCO, CLIP prefers the correct shorter description only 34.0% of the time, and performance drops to 27.8% when the added detail is a relation. We trace this vulnerability to weak supervision on caption parts: contrastive training aligns full sentences but does not explicitly enforce that individual entities and relations are grounded. We propose CS-CLIP (Component-Supervised CLIP), which decomposes captions into entity and relation units, constructs a minimally edited foil for each unit, and fine-tunes the model to score the correct unit above its foil while preserving standard dual-encoder inference. CS-CLIP raises half-truth accuracy to 76.4% and improves average performance on established compositional benchmarks by 5.8 points, suggesting that reducing half-truth errors aligns with broader gains in compositional understanding.
